title: The Pigeonhole Principle
short: If more than k · n items go into n boxes, some box gets at least k + 1; to guarantee something, plan for the worst case.
trouble: Students find the number that makes a repeat possible instead of the number that guarantees one, which is one more than the worst case.

blocks.html: Some counting questions ask for a guarantee rather than a count: how many socks must you grab to be sure of a pair? The answer comes from a principle so simple it sounds obvious, yet it settles surprising questions. It is a fact about functions between finite sets, and it is usually combined with the sum and product rules.

Pigeonhole principle: if more than $n$ items go into $n$ boxes, some box gets at least two. More generally, if more than $kn$ items go into $n$ boxes, some box gets at least $k + 1$; with $N$ items, some box gets at least $\lceil N/n \rceil$. To find the number that guarantees an outcome, find the largest number that can still avoid it (the worst case) and add one.

Prove it by contrapositive: if every box held at most $k$ items, the total would be at most $kn$. So more than $kn$ items force a box above $k$. In function language: a function from a bigger finite set to a smaller one cannot be one-to-one. Two inputs must share an output.

blocks.name: disc-relation
blocks.cap: Five inputs, four outputs: however the arrows are drawn, some output is hit twice. Try to rearrange them to avoid it.

blocks.title: Socks in the dark
blocks.q: A drawer has many socks in $4$ colors. How many must you take, without looking, to be sure of two of the same color? Three of the same color?
steps: Two: the worst case is one of each color, $4$ socks with no pair. The next sock must match: $5$.
Three: the worst case is two of each color, $8$ socks. The next one makes three of some color: $9$.

blocks.title: Birth months
blocks.q: Among $100$ people, what is the largest number you can be sure share a birth month?
steps: $12$ months are the boxes. If each month had at most $8$ people, there would be at most $96$ people.
So some month has at least $\lceil 100/12 \rceil = 9$.
And $9$ is the best guarantee: the people could be spread with $8$ or $9$ in each month.

blocks.title: Pairs that add to $11$
blocks.q: Show that among any $6$ numbers chosen from $\{1, 2, \ldots, 10\}$, two add up to $11$.
steps: $6$ numbers in $5$ boxes: some box receives two numbers, and those two add to $11$.
With only $5$ numbers it can fail: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$.
blocks.a: $6$ numbers always contain such a pair.

blocks.html: Finding the number that makes something possible instead of the number that guarantees it. With $4$ colors, $2$ socks might match, but nothing is certain until $5$. Check: build the worst case on purpose, the largest set of items that avoids the goal, and confirm that one more item cannot avoid it. The answer is the worst case plus one.
